title: T-money Card and the Seoul Subway: A Beginner's Guide
html:
If you're coming to Korea for the first time, one little plastic card will make your trip so much easier: the T-money card. It works on subways, city buses, and even some taxis and convenience stores, all over the country. This guide explains exactly what it is, how to get one, and how to use it — plus the basics of how the Seoul subway works, step by step.

What is a T-money card?

A T-money card is a rechargeable payment card, a bit like a prepaid debit card just for transportation (and small purchases). You load money onto it, then tap it on a reader every time you ride the subway or a bus. No need to figure out ticket machines or buy a new ticket for every single ride.

T-money brand logo. Credit: Tmoney Global, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Source.

Where to buy a T-money card

  • Convenience stores: CU, GS25, 7-Eleven, and other convenience stores near subway stations sell T-money cards for about ₩2,500–₩4,000. Just ask the staff for a "T-money card."
  • Incheon Airport: You can buy one right after you land, at convenience stores or transportation counters in arrivals.
  • Subway station machines: Ticket machines at subway stations also sell T-money cards, with an English menu option.

Tip: buying the card is separate from loading money onto it. The ₩2,500–4,000 you pay is just for the physical card itself — you still need to add travel credit on top.

How to load (top up) money

  • At a convenience store: Hand your card to the cashier and tell them how much to add, then pay in cash. Most convenience store registers cannot load T-money using a foreign credit card — cash only.
  • At subway station kiosks: Look for a "T-money Card / Charge" machine near the ticket gates. Many of these now accept foreign Visa, Mastercard, and other international cards, so this is the easiest option if you don't have Korean cash yet.
  • On your phone: If you have a newer iPhone, you can add a T-money card to Apple Wallet and top it up with a foreign card, then simply tap your phone at the gate instead of carrying a plastic card.

You can usually load anywhere from ₩1,000 to ₩90,000 at a time. Load a bit more than you think you'll need — running out of balance mid-trip means an awkward stop at the gate.

How the Seoul subway works

Seoul's subway is one of the easiest parts of visiting Korea, once you know a few basics:

  • Lines are numbered and color-coded. Line 1 is dark blue, Line 2 is green, and so on. Station signs, maps, and announcements all use these colors and numbers, so you don't need to read Korean to follow along.
  • Tap in, tap out. Tap your T-money card on the reader at the gate when you enter, and tap again when you exit. The fare is calculated automatically based on the distance you traveled.
  • Transfers are usually free. If you switch to another subway line, or from subway to bus, within about 30 minutes and without leaving through the exit gates, you generally won't pay an extra base fare — just any small distance-based difference.
  • Use a map app. Google Maps does not give reliable walking or transit directions inside Korea. Use Naver Map or KakaoMap instead (both have English versions) — they'll tell you exactly which line, which platform side, and which exit number to use.

Platform at Seoul Station, Line 4. Credit: Mobius6, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Source.

No card yet? You can still ride with a paper ticket

If you don't want to buy a T-money card just for a single ride, every station has ticket machines with an English option for a "single journey ticket." Here's how it works:

  • Choose your destination on the machine and pay the fare plus a ₩500 deposit.
  • The machine gives you a small plastic token — tap it on the gate reader just like a T-money card.
  • When you arrive, look for a grey "deposit refund" machine near the exit gates (usually within a few steps of the ticket machines) and insert the token to get your ₩500 back.

This works fine for a one-off trip, but it's slower than a T-money card if you're taking the subway more than once or twice, since you have to repeat the whole process every ride.

Practical tips

  • You don't need a separate bus card. The same T-money card works on city buses, intercity buses, and many taxis too.
  • Keep it somewhere you can tap easily — a phone case card slot or a small pouch works well, since you'll be tapping in and out constantly.
  • Before you fly home, you can get most of your remaining balance refunded in cash at a convenience store (a small handling fee applies over a certain amount), so you're not left with unused Korean won on a card.
  • Rush hour is roughly 7–9am and 6–8pm on weekdays. Trains are extremely crowded during these times, especially on Line 2. If you have flexibility, try to travel outside these windows, especially with luggage.

Once you've got a T-money card in hand and know how to tap in and out, getting around Seoul (and most other Korean cities) becomes one of the easiest parts of the trip.
